question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study uses participatory co-design workshops with children (including those with SBMD) and circus professionals to create playful exergames while simultaneously collecting data for a machine learning model intended for healthy exercise and assistive-technology purposes. The design probe Cirkus is explicitly framed to support co-creating movement-based games (fun) and to collect movement data for a bespoke ML model for health-related exercise (utility). Stakeholders are diverse (children with and without SBMD, circus professionals, researchers), and the paper emphasizes both playful motivation and serious health/assistive aims, matching a 'both fun and utility first' design with diverse stakeholders.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The described activities are structured games with explicit goals, competition, and rules (e.g., obstacle course race inspired by Temple Run, team battles for points, Animal Tag with rule variations). However, they are also designed to be flexible and reconfigurable (multiple configurations, negotiable roles, variations in rules), matching a flexible structure with rules rather than a rigid ruleset.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The games are exergames where children intentionally perform specific animal movements, race through obstacle courses, and compete on time or points. Success depends largely on players’ physical skill, speed, and choice of movement (e.g., picking faster animals to cross the room), with no indication of randomizing devices like dice or card draws. While an inaccurate ML classifier is used playfully as an antagonist in some games, the core mechanics remain performance- and skill-based rather than chance-driven, suggesting a mostly (but not purely) skill-based design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The Cirkus design probe supports games where multiple children play together, negotiate roles (e.g., hunter and hunted), and interact socially, while the technology provides individual movement recording and feedback. This indicates a mix of solo (individual movement performance, data collection, feedback) and social affordances (group games, negotiation, co-located play), matching category 3.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The paper explicitly notes that some games are turn-based while others are simultaneous. The focal example described in detail, Animal Crossing (a Red Light Green Light variant), involves all children choosing an animal and moving forward at the same time each round, which is an entirely simultaneous action structure. Given the mixed catalog but needing a single best-fit for the study’s design, the clearest described mechanics align with simultaneous play.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The paper’s design probe (Cirkus) is explicitly built to support many different exergames, some of which are turn-based and some simultaneous, indicating both asynchronous and synchronous play. The framework and examples (e.g., Food Chain requiring negotiation outside the app plus in-game simultaneous movement) suggest a roughly balanced mix of synchronous (real-time movement, timing-based elimination) and asynchronous (turn-based structures, rating, configuration, negotiation) affordances across the catalog of games rather than being dominated by one or the other.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study’s games include both competitive elements (racing to treasure, competing for best time, teams battling for most points, first to reach the other side) and collaborative elements (groups of children collaborating to create hybrid animals, co-creating games). This indicates a mix of competitive and collaborative play rather than being mostly or entirely one or the other.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: Across the catalog of 17 animal-locomotion exergames, some games have all players using similar roles and actions (e.g., Animal Crossing / Animal Tournament where everyone chooses an animal and advances similarly), while others explicitly introduce differing roles or relationships (e.g., Food Chain with hunter vs hunted, app vs players, or games pitting the application against players). This mix of shared structures with differentiated roles and objectives indicates a design space that includes both symmetrical and asymmetrical games rather than being purely one or the other.
